title: The Myth of 'Disruptive Innovation'

dom.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions

st.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis by distinguishing industrial change from Christensen’s specific causal mechanism, reporting weak conformity among the theory’s cited cases, and arguing that selective cases and retrospective recalibration undermine generalisability and predictive testing.

kp.k: Disruption theory specifies a mechanism, not merely competition
kp.d: The article distinguishes loose uses of disruption from Christensen's specific theory: entrants adopt technologies initially serving niche markets; technologically capable incumbents prioritize core customers rather than invest; improving entrant technologies subsequently displace incumbents. This is a management-theory source, not direct evidence about AI or legal services.
qs: Upstart companies adopt a new technology that appeals to a niche market rather than the market that dominant players focus on.
The dominant players have the technological savvy to compete, but, instead, they listen to their core customers and fail to invest in the new technology.
The new technology then improves at a rapid rate, and the upstarts displace the older companies.

kp.k: Original disk-drive evidence is itself disputed
kp.d: The article reports that Goldfarb and Andrew A. King dispute whether Christensen's proposed dynamics occurred in disk drives. A 2002 paper by King and Christopher L. Tucci found that firms with more experience in existing markets were more likely to enter new markets, contrary to the proposed experience-induced myopia.
qs: Far from experience leading to myopia, King and Christopher L. Tucci found in a 2002 paper, disk-drive firms with the most experience in existing markets were actually more likely to enter new ones.

kp.k: Goldfarb challenges generalization and demands cross-industry testing
kp.d: Goldfarb argues that even a factually correct original study could establish, at most, an industry-specific finding. He calls for replication using a reasonable sampling strategy across industries to identify applicability and conditions, and claims such rigorous testing had not been done.
qs: Generalizing to the universe of industries based on the study of a single industry is simply wrong,
The next step would have been to replicate that study across many industries, with a reasonable sampling strategy that would tell us more about when it applies and when it doesn't.

would be to take several industries based upon certain criteria — say, high tech, low tech, manufacturing and services — and then explore the predictive validity of the theory of disruption across these industries.

kp.k: Selective cases and recalibration undermine falsifiability
kp.d: Goldfarb alleges that Christensen selects cases featuring incumbents losing to entrants and adjusts the theory when contrary cases arise. This is Goldfarb's methodological criticism, rather than an independently established finding presented by the article.
qs: Instead, Christensen has assembled a series of case studies sampled on, as far as I can tell, incumbents losing to new entrants.
When a case appears that does not comport, the strategy is to calibrate the theory to the data.
This is a great strategy for lengthening the longevity of a theory but does not subject the theory to Popperian refutability.

kp.k: Few cited disruption cases meet all defining features
kp.d: The article reports that King and Baljir Baatartogtokh's Fall 2015 MIT Sloan Management Review paper examined 77 cases offered by Christensen and co-authors, interviewing experts in the relevant fields. Only 9 percent exhibited all four specified features: successful incumbent sustaining innovation, overshooting substantial customer needs, capability to respond to entrants, and subsequent incumbent floundering. In 39 percent, incumbents survived or thrived.
qs: only 9 percent of the 77 case studies that Christensen and his co-authors have presented as examples of disruption actually show all four of the features that supposedly define a disruptive event.
Fully 39 percent of the time, for instance, incumbents survived or even thrived after being disrupted, King and Baatartogtokh found.
The authors' methodology was to interview experts in the field from which the case studies were drawn.

kp.k: Incumbents cannot necessarily respond to every technological threat
kp.d: Goldfarb challenges the assumption that incumbents possess the ability to counter every threat. The article questions whether the Post Office could plausibly have reinvented itself as an email provider when AOL-backed email threatened traditional mail, presenting this as a doubtful counterfactual rather than a measured finding.
qs: One notable and problematic assumption of the theory, according to Goldfarb, is that incumbent entities have the ability to respond to every threat.
When email, backed by AOL, arose as a threat to traditional mail service, could the Post Office have plausibly reinvented itself as an email provider, as Christensen has implied? It seems doubtful.

kp.k: Diversification offers an alternative explanation for Fuji's response
kp.d: Goldfarb disputes the interpretation that Fuji Film Holding Corp. outflanked Eastman Kodak by anticipating digital cameras' disruptive effects on film. He instead attributes its response to anticipating digital-camera commoditization and diversifying into coatings, cosmetics and document processing.
qs: Fuji Film Holding Corp. did not outflank Eastman Kodak because it foresaw the disruptive impact of digital cameras on film.
Rather, it recognized that digital cameras were on the road to becoming a commodity, and so it moved into other areas, including coatings, cosmetics and document processing.

kp.k: Capable incumbents often compete rather than ignore entrants
kp.d: The article asserts that incumbents usually compete when able, illustrating the point with electric vehicles as of September 2015. Against claims that Tesla was disrupting automobiles, it identifies Ford, Nissan, GM and Porsche among competing established manufacturers; the example does not establish eventual competitive outcomes.
qs: When incumbents can compete with insurgents, they usually do.
Tesla is often said to be disrupting the car industry, but Ford, Nissan, GM, Porsche and a host of other companies are all racing to win the electric-car race.

kp.k: Strategic-management findings face broader replication concerns
kp.d: The article reports a forthcoming Goldfarb and King paper suggesting that 26 to 40 percent of results in strategic-management journals would not recur if experiments were replicated. This is a reported estimate of non-replication, not a description of completed replications. The article attributes the problem mainly to seeing patterns in complex data and some self-interest, rather than conscious fraud.
qs: In a forthcoming paper, Goldfarb and King suggested that 26 to 40 percent of the results in strategic-management journals would not reappear if the experiments were replicated.
This is almost never conscious fraud, but rather a too-human desire to see patterns in complex data, where none exist (plus a smidgen of self-interest).

kp.k: Publication credibility and disciplinary investment reinforce theory acceptance
kp.d: Goldfarb attributes disruption theory's acceptance partly to cognitive and sociological mechanisms: publication confers excessive credibility, knowledgeable insiders become invested in defending the theory, and skeptical outsiders lack time to examine its evidence.
qs: It's a general problem that once something is published, it gets an extra credence that it should not have,
Then there's the sociological problem that people who know the theory best become invested in defending it, rather than challenging it.
Meanwhile, people outside the subfield, who may be skeptical, "don't have time to investigate the evidence."

kp.k: Rejecting Christensen's mechanism does not deny industrial disruption
kp.d: Goldfarb explicitly accepts that industries undergo disruption while rejecting Christensen's explanation of how it happens. His conclusion is that the theory acts as a thinking shortcut that obscures the reasons firms survive or fail during change.
qs: I wouldn't at all state that industries don't get disrupted,
They do. It's just the mechanism does not work in the way Christensen has described.
Disruption theory serves as a "thinking shortcut" that obscures, rather than clarifies, why some firms thrive during periods of change, and others die, he says.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This cross-domain source makes no claims about AI or legal services. Its central claim, attributed to Brent Goldfarb, is that technological disruption occurs but does not generally follow Christensen's proposed mechanism.
pts.d: Goldfarb challenges the proposition that capable incumbents systematically neglect niche technologies because they listen to existing customers, then lose to entrants as those technologies improve. He argues that the theory lacks rigorous cross-industry validation and obscures differences in firms' responses to technological change. The article presents Christensen's mechanism as the target of this critique, not as its own endorsed prediction.

pts.k: The article argues that incumbents often compete when they can, and that survival can depend on diversification rather than anticipating and adopting a supposedly disruptive technology.
pts.d: The article describes established carmakers competing in electric vehicles rather than ignoring Tesla. Goldfarb questions whether the Post Office could plausibly have become an email provider, challenging the assumption that incumbents can respond to every technological threat. He also attributes Fuji's response to digital photography to recognising commoditisation and diversifying, rather than simply foreseeing digital cameras' impact on film. These are examples and conditional claims, not forecasts of inevitable incumbent survival.

pts.k: Goldfarb argues that publication credibility, cognitive biases and professional investment sustain acceptance of weakly tested management theories; a forthcoming paper estimates substantial non-replication in strategic-management research.
pts.d: The article attributes to Goldfarb and King an estimate that 26–40 percent of results in strategic-management journals would not recur on replication. It does not describe the estimation method or report completed replications establishing that percentage. Goldfarb separately argues that publication gives claims excessive credibility and that specialists become invested in defending theories. The article presents pattern-seeking and self-interest, rather than usually conscious fraud, as explanations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source supports its critique with a reported expert-interview review of 77 disruption cases, an earlier disk-drive study, and illustrative industry examples.
pts.d: The article reports that Andrew A. King and Baljir Baatartogtokh's Fall 2015 MIT Sloan Management Review paper found all four specified disruption features in only 9 percent of 77 cases, while incumbents survived or thrived in 39 percent. The four features concerned successful sustaining innovation, overshooting customer needs, incumbent capacity to respond, and subsequent incumbent failure. The review interviewed domain experts; these percentages concern selected disruption case studies, not a representative estimate of failure across industries. The article also reports that King and Christopher L. Tucci's 2002 paper found more experienced disk-drive firms more likely to enter new markets. Postal services, Fuji/Kodak and electric vehicles provide additional examples rather than systematic tests.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims are retrospective and contemporaneous as of 15 September 2015, with no dated forecast of industry displacement.
pts.d: The article examines a theory developed in the 1990s, cites a 2002 disk-drive study and a Fall 2015 case review, and describes electric-vehicle competition as ongoing. The replication estimate concerns a paper forthcoming at publication and is conditional on experiments being replicated. Goldfarb explicitly distinguishes evidence about one industry from a general claim and calls for sampling across industries to establish applicability and boundary conditions. The claim that incumbents usually compete is expressly conditional on their ability to do so.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are incumbent firms, entrants, business leaders and management researchers, not legal-sector actors.
pts.d: Incumbents in disk drives, postal services, photography and automobiles face differing possibilities of entry into new markets, direct technological competition, diversification, survival or failure. New entrants are competitors whose success should not be assumed to follow a universal displacement mechanism. Business leaders risk relying on an oversimplified account of technological change. Management researchers and theory specialists are described as susceptible to publication credibility and incentives to defend established ideas, while outsiders lack time to examine the evidence. No consequences for lawyers, law firms or legal clients are specified.
